implementation_notes: Go has no ring buffer in the standard library, and the idiomatic answer for a queue is a channel - which is internally a ring buffer with two wait queues (the runtime's hchan has a ring buffer dataqsiz with sendx/recvx indices and two wait queues). So in most Go programs the runtime already provides the circular buffer and you should use a buffered channel. Where a hand-written ring is right is a fixed-size, no-chunk, allocation-free hot path (an audio ring, a lock-free SPSC queue where a channel's channel-send overhead and per-send function call is too heavy). Go's garbage collector also makes the 'no allocation' benefit less compelling than in C, and a buffered channel allocates its buffer once at make(chan T, n) and never grows. For a true SPSC ring, the two indices as uint64 atomics with acquire/release, padded, is the construction.
idiom_name: buffered channel (the runtime's own ring buffer) for most cases; hand-written uint64 SPSC ring for a fixed, allocation-free hot path
pitfalls: In Go, atomics are all sequentially consistent (no acquire/release), so the ring's ordering is stronger than needed - correct but slightly costlier than the C/Rust form.

A buffered channel is the runtime's ring buffer already; hand-rolling one to 'save the channel overhead' is only justified on a measured hot path, because a channel send is a function call plus a lock.
The pad fields between head and tail are needed on a cache-coherent machine or the ping-pong dominates; without them the 'lock-free' ring is slower than the channel it replaced.

Go's GC means 'no allocation after construction' matters less than in C, and make(chan T, n) already allocates its buffer once - so a hand-written ring's main win is the absent channel-send overhead, not the allocation.
